groups.text: Here is a card fee in Java and Kotlin: the amount times the rate in basis points, over ten thousand.
java P shows what java C made of the Java one.
Seven instructions, and not one variable name.
It reads like noise, until you see the machine it runs on.
Each call gets a frame.
Numbered slots hold the local variables.
The operand stack is a pile: instructions pop their inputs off the top, and push their results back.
Call it with one two five zero zero zero cents and two hundred ninety basis points.
amountMinor is a long, and a long fills two slots.
So which slot does bps get?
Pause on it.
Slot two. That's why the listing says iload_two.
Now run it.
lload_zero copies the long from slot zero onto the stack: the l is for long.
iload_two copies the int from slot two: the i is for int.
Next is a multiply, and lmul only takes two longs.
The top of the stack is an int.
What has to happen first?
itwol, int to long.
It pops the two hundred ninety and pushes it back as a long, two slots tall.
lmul pops both longs and pushes the product.
ldctwo_w pushes the long one zero zero zero zero from the constant pool.
ldiv pops two longs and pushes three thousand six hundred twenty-five.
lreturn pops it and returns it: thirty-six euros and twenty-five cents.
At its fullest, the stack held two longs, four slots.
java P -v prints that as stack=four, and the slots as locals=three.
kotlinc's version is almost the same: a public static final method, on a class named StackDemoKt.
Only the constant differs.
java C loads a ready-made long from the constant pool.
kotlinc writes one zero zero zero zero into the instruction with sipush, then widens it with itwol.
Same long on the stack.
The rule: every instruction pops typed inputs off the stack and pushes its result, and its first letter names the type.
A quick check.
Add plus thirty at the end of the Java version.
What appears between ldiv and lreturn?
ldctwo_w pushes the long thirty, then ladd adds the two longs.
